What if imagining movement were enough to control a machine?

Building a neural interface that works without an implant is difficult. Brain signals weaken by the time they reach a headset and become mixed with electrical activity from facial movements and nearby electronics. Implants get a cleaner reading because they sit closer to the brain.

Synaptrix uses an EEG headset to capture brain activity linked to imagined movement. Its large motor models decode intended movement from those signals and turn it into commands for a device.

The first application is wheelchair control. Synaptrix says users can steer by imagining where they want to go. It also says its signal-processing accuracy and denoising performance have held up on busy New York streets. For non-invasive control to be useful in daily life, it has to work beyond a shielded lab.

Synaptrix says it has already brought the same system to freely moving cursor control. Steering a wheelchair and moving a cursor require different commands, but both begin with decoding intended movement. If the models can handle that intent across more people and settings, prosthetics and other devices could follow.

Wheelchair use gives Synaptrix real world data on how intended movement appears across people and conditions. As more headsets and applications come online, that dataset can widen and the models trained on it can improve.

Better decoding could make the system useful on still more devices. The wheelchair shows what the system can do today. The data and models built through real world use could determine how far it goes.

(Original content provided by @august_wstein & @DrewAHenderson at Delphi Ventures)

Lets say you're buying BTC with USDT

you look at the mid price of BTC right now and see that 10k USDT = 0.1 BTC

But you can't execute at mid price, so you look at the orderbook and calculate 'if i executed a 10k market order, which orders would i fill and how much BTC would I get'

You calculation returns that you'd get 0.0999 BTC, which means 10$ less than mid price, 10$ is your predicted slippage

Then you execute the 10k market order, and you get 0.0998 BTC, that's 20$ less than the mid price

20$ is your realized slippage

@arc mainnet goes live today.

Here are 6 projects I’m watching before the timeline catches up:

1. Tolly ($TOLLY): Launchpad + trading terminal

@TollyLabs combines a launchpad, a trading terminal and onchain analytics. It has already done roughly $4.9M in volume across 46K trades.

Part of the fees goes toward $TOLLY buybacks and burns, with around 28.9M TOLLY already removed from circulation.

2. Long ($LONG): Stock-paired memecoin launchpad

@Longdotsupply wants to pair memes with tokenized stocks, taking the Robinhood stock / meme experiment onto Arc.

I find this more interesting than another standard meme launcher, though it depends on whether tokenized stocks actually gain traction on the chain.

3. Arguspad ($ARGUS): Memecoin launchpad

@Arguspad is a straightforward memecoin launchpad. I’m watching whether it starts producing actual runners.

One or two successful launches can change where traders spend their time, but I’d want to see that happen before getting too excited about $ARGUS.

4. Warp ($WARP): Cross-chain USDC launchpad

@circlewarp combines a launchpad and trading terminal with cross-chain USDC transfers through CCTP.

The appeal is being able to move USDC from another chain and trade tokens on Arc without going through three different apps.

5. Archemist: X-based token launcher

@Archemistdotfun lets you launch tokens through an X bot. Its V4 setup includes anti-snipe mechanics, creator buys, buybacks and holder rewards.

I’m curious how the anti-snipe mechanics work in practice once people are trading with real money.

6. ArcDEXScan: Scanner + aggregator

@ArcDEXScan combines a scanner, aggregator and launchpad. This is one I’d keep open even without buying anything through it.

If launches end up spread across 20 different venues, having somewhere to see what’s moving would save a lot of digging.

For the first few days, I’d stick to official Arc / USDC routes once they’re live, use a fresh wallet and avoid unlimited approvals.

I wouldn’t try to guess Arc’s $PONS before the market opens. I’d rather see which venues get real volume and whether their launches hold up.

Anyway, this is a "watchlist" and not recommendation to buy.

Market's tanking + new chain + early stage projects = high risk.

Do you like $INTC ?

I believe Intel has had several significant positive developments over the past month. The stock appears to have bottomed around $85 and now trades near $97.

Yesterday, I opened the following trade, which expires on November 20:

Buy one $95 call.
Sell three $130 calls.
Sell one $80 put.

The maximum profit is around $130, meaning Intel would need to rise approximately 33% by November 20. On the downside, I only start losing if Intel falls more than 20%, at which point I would be assigned the shares at $80. On the upside, the trade remains profitable unless Intel rises more than approximately 51% from that point you start loosing money.

My logic is as follows: 

1) We are entering a period of weak seasonality, which is usually a difficult time for the stock market. That is one reason I feel comfortable selling the three $130 calls, I intentionally want to waste time.

2) On the other hand, Intel has had several positive developments recently. That is why I also feel comfortable selling the $80 put.

That is the basic logic behind the trade: I am positive on Intel, but I am not expecting an extreme move higher by November 20. The sweet spot is a ~35% rise in the next 66 days, with the maximum profit around $130.

You could also view this trade as an add-on to an existing Intel position. Let’s say Intel currently represents 5% of your portfolio. If the stock rises “only” to $130, you will make money on both the options and the stock. If it rises 50% to $150, you will still be very happy because of the profit on your shares, despite not making money on the options trade.

If Intel falls to $80, perhaps that is a price at which you would feel comfortable doubling your position. You receive additional shares at a price you like and continue holding them because you believe Intel should perform well over the long term.

Remember, this is just an idea, not a recommendation. You might want to choose different strikes or expiration.

Biotech Contemplation

I recently wrote that our biotech expert likes $IONS. But the more time I spend around biotech, the harder it becomes for me to recommend companies with major Phase 3 trials ahead of them.

Unless you run a dedicated biotech fund, there are several problems.

You can wake up one morning and discover that another company’s similar drug has failed. Suddenly, your stock is down 10%, 20%, or even 30% because of a negative read-through, without giving you any chance to react.

That kind of risk also limits how large the position can be. And the more I think about it, the more I believe that owning a stock at just 1% or 2% of your portfolio is mostly a waste of time. But if the stock can fall 30% overnight because of another company’s trial, it is very difficult to build a meaningful position.

It is true that we have had some big biotech winners. But I also see the losers, and more importantly, I see how difficult it is to put serious money into these companies while controlling the risk.

Going forward, I will still publish ideas from our biotech expert and I will mention they come from our biotech expert because the medicine is interesting and his research is valuable. But my own focus will be mainly on companies I research myself and reach my own conclusions on, such as $URGN after they passed their phase 3 and $WGS.

I will generally avoid companies like $IONS and other biotech names I have discussed in the past, unless they are already profitable, generating real cash, and do not have major Phase 3 risks hanging over them.

I said it before, and I continue to stand by it: Kevin Warsh will do what he believes is best for the markets. He is probably the most market-friendly Fed governor we have ever had.

Now I am telling you again: Warsh will pursue what he considers the most balanced path for the Fed, interest rates, the economy, AND THE FINANCIAL MARKETS. The probability that he will knowingly do anything that, in his judgment, could seriously damage the market is extremely low.
